uncited: Texture Splatting is a volume rendering technique that represents volumetric data or point clouds as a set of texture-mapped primitives (typically quads or squares) rasterized onto the screen.

It solves the problem of rendering high-frequency detail and complex scalar/vector fields efficiently by offloading the reconstruction kernel evaluation to the fragment shader via texture lookups, rather than computing per-fragment kernel values analytically.

It sets itself apart from standard Gaussian Splatting by using texture maps to store color, normal, or other per-fragment properties, allowing for higher fidelity with fewer primitives and avoiding the artifacts associated with polygonal mesh approximations of Gaussian kernels.
For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening .
Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) .
Texture Splatting originated as a technique to render large datasets efficiently by leveraging texture hardware.
The technique has been widely adopted in scientific visualization and real-time rendering for its balance of performance and visual quality.
